+ import { create } from 'zustand'
+ import type { VoiceCard } from '../../../shared/voice'
+ import { VoiceReply } from '../../../shared/voiceReply'
+ import { agentsHere, agentToAsk } from '../design/askAgent'
+ import { VoiceEar } from '../media/voice/ear'
+ import { VoiceListener } from '../media/voice/listener'
+ import { progressOf, rememberVoice, storedVoice, type Fetching } from '../media/voice/models'
+ import { VoiceMouth } from '../media/voice/mouth'
+ import { endOf, findTurn, textOf, worthSending } from '../media/voice/turn'
+ import { playSound } from '../media/sounds'
+ import { useCrew } from './store'
+ 
+ // off       nobody is talking
+ // waking    the two models are being fetched, the first time only
+ // listening the microphone is open and the room is quiet
+ // hearing   somebody is talking right now
+ // thinking  what they said has gone to the agent
+ // speaking  the answer is coming out of the speakers
+ export type VoicePhase = 'off' | 'waking' | 'listening' | 'hearing' | 'thinking' | 'speaking'
+ 
+ const AGENT_KEY = 'crew.voice.agent'
+ 
+ export interface VoiceState {
+   open: boolean
+   phase: VoicePhase
+   agentId: string | null
+   threadId: string | null
+   progress: number
+   // The last thing this machine heard somebody say, and the sentence coming
+   // out of the speakers now. One caption each, because they are two people.
+   heard: string
+   saying: string
+   cards: VoiceCard[]
+   muted: boolean
+   voice: string
+   problem: string | null
+   start: (agentId?: string) => Promise<void>
+   end: () => void
+   toggleMute: () => void
+   pickVoice: (id: string) => void
+   pickAgent: (agentId: string) => void
+   answer: (text: string) => void
+   clearProblem: () => void
+ }
+ 
+ const REST = {
+   phase: 'off' as VoicePhase,
+   threadId: null,
+   progress: 0,
+   heard: '',
+   saying: '',
+   cards: [] as VoiceCard[],
+   problem: null
+ }
+ 
+ const storedAgent = (): string | null => globalThis.localStorage?.getItem(AGENT_KEY) ?? null
+ 
+ export const useVoice = create<VoiceState>((set, get) => {
+   const fetching = new Map<string, Fetching>()
+   let unwatch: (() => void) | null = null
+   let promptId: string | null = null
+   let reply: VoiceReply | null = null
+   let asked: string | null = null
+   let raw = ''
+   let ready = 0
+ 
+   const fetched = (file: string, loaded: number, total: number) => {
+     fetching.set(file, { file, loaded, total })
+     if (get().phase === 'waking') set({ progress: progressOf(fetching) })
+   }
+ 
+   // Both models have to be here before the microphone is worth opening. Two
+   // downloads fill one ring, so it never jumps back to the start halfway.
+   const woke = () => {
+     ready++
+     if (ready < 2 || get().phase !== 'waking') return
+     set({ phase: 'listening', progress: 1 })
+   }
+ 
+   const listener = new VoiceListener({
+     onFetching: fetched,
+     onReady: woke,
+     onFailed: message => get().phase !== 'off' && set({ problem: message })
+   })
+ 
+   const mouth = new VoiceMouth({
+     onFetching: fetched,
+     onReady: woke,
+     onSaying: saying => set({ saying, phase: 'speaking' }),
+     onQuiet: () => {
+       if (get().phase === 'speaking') set({ phase: 'listening', saying: '' })
+     },
+     onFailed: message => get().phase !== 'off' && set({ problem: message })
+   })
+ 
+   const ear = new VoiceEar({
+     onStart: () => {
+       if (get().phase === 'off' || get().phase === 'waking') return
+       // Cutting in stops the voice and nothing else. Whatever the agent is
+       // doing to the project it goes on doing, because an interruption is
+       // somebody talking over an answer, not somebody undoing work.
+       if (mouth.speaking) {
+         promptId = null
+         reply = null
+         mouth.stop()
+       }
+       set({ phase: 'hearing', saying: '' })
+     },
+     onEnd: audio => void heard(audio)
+   })
+ 
+   const heard = async (audio: Float32Array) => {
+     if (get().phase === 'off') return
+     set({ phase: 'thinking' })
+     const text = await listener.hear(audio)
+     if (get().phase === 'off') return
+     if (!worthSending(text)) {
+       set({ phase: 'listening' })
+       return
+     }
+     set({ heard: text })
+     send(text)
+   }
+ 
+   const send = (text: string) => {
+     const { threadId, agentId } = get()
+     if (!agentId) return
+     asked = text
+     promptId = null
+     raw = ''
+     reply = new VoiceReply()
+     set({ phase: 'thinking', cards: [], saying: '' })
+     mouth.open(get().voice)
+     const crew = useCrew.getState()
+     if (threadId) crew.sendChat(text, threadId)
+     else crew.sendChat(text, undefined, undefined, undefined, [agentId], ['voice'])
+   }
+ 
+   const speak = (say: string, cards: VoiceCard[]) => {
+     if (say) mouth.push(say)
+     if (cards.length > 0) set(state => ({ cards: [...state.cards, ...cards] }))
+   }
+ 
+   const watch = () =>
+     useCrew.subscribe(crew => {
+       const state = get()
+       if (state.phase === 'off' || !state.agentId) return
+       if (!promptId && asked) {
+         const turn = findTurn(crew.events, {
+           byName: crew.selfName,
+           agentId: state.agentId,
+           text: asked,
+           threadId: state.threadId
+         })
+         if (!turn) return
+         promptId = turn.promptId
+         if (!state.threadId) set({ threadId: turn.threadId })
+       }
+       if (!promptId || !reply) return
+       const grown = textOf(crew.steps[promptId])
+       if (grown.length > raw.length) {
+         raw = grown
+         const { say, cards } = reply.grew(raw)
+         speak(say, cards)
+       }
+       const ended = endOf(crew.events, promptId)
+       if (!ended) return
+       // The last text step and the end of the run say the same thing, so the
+       // one that reaches further is the whole of it. A run that failed says so
+       // out loud rather than leaving the orb listening to nothing.
+       const whole = ended.ok && ended.text.startsWith(raw) ? ended.text : raw
+       const { say, cards } = reply.whole(whole || ended.text)
+       speak(say, cards)
+       if (!ended.ok && !say) mouth.push('That did not work.')
+       promptId = null
+       reply = null
+       asked = null
+       raw = ''
+       mouth.seal()
+       if (!mouth.speaking) set({ phase: 'listening' })
+     })
+ 
+   return {
+     open: false,
+     agentId: null,
+     muted: false,
+     voice: storedVoice(),
+     ...REST,
+ 
+     start: async agentId => {
+       if (get().open) return
+       const agents = useCrew.getState().agents
+       const picked = agentToAsk(agents, agentId ?? storedAgent())
+       if (!picked) {
+         set({ open: true, ...REST, problem: 'No agent is here to talk to.' })
+         return
+       }
+       playSound('join')
+       set({ open: true, ...REST, agentId: picked.id, phase: 'waking', muted: false })
+       fetching.clear()
+       ready = 0
+       unwatch = watch()
+       listener.load()
+       mouth.load()
+       const problem = await ear.open()
+       if (get().phase === 'off') return ear.close()
+       if (problem) {
+         set({ problem: 'crew could not reach your microphone. Check its permission in System Settings.' })
+       }
+     },
+ 
+     end: () => {
+       if (!get().open) return
+       playSound('leave')
+       unwatch?.()
+       unwatch = null
+       promptId = null
+       reply = null
+       asked = null
+       raw = ''
+       ear.close()
+       mouth.stop()
+       listener.forget()
+       set({ open: false, ...REST })
+     },
+ 
+     toggleMute: () => {
+       const muted = !get().muted
+       ear.mute(muted)
+       set({ muted })
+       if (muted && get().phase === 'hearing') set({ phase: 'listening' })
+     },
+ 
+     pickVoice: id => {
+       rememberVoice(id)
+       set({ voice: id })
+     },
+ 
+     // Changing who you are talking to starts the conversation again, because a
+     // thread belongs to one agent and half a conversation is not context.
+     pickAgent: agentId => {
+       if (agentId === get().agentId) return
+       try {
+         globalThis.localStorage?.setItem(AGENT_KEY, agentId)
+       } catch {
+         // Storage turned off keeps the choice for this conversation.
+       }
+       mouth.stop()
+       promptId = null
+       reply = null
+       asked = null
+       raw = ''
+       set({ agentId, threadId: null, cards: [], heard: '', saying: '', phase: 'listening' })
+     },
+ 
+     // A tapped option, or anything typed. It goes in as a turn of its own, so
+     // picking one off a card reads back the way saying it would have.
+     answer: text => {
+       const clean = text.trim()
+       if (!clean || get().phase === 'off') return
+       mouth.stop()
+       set({ heard: clean })
+       send(clean)
+     },
+ 
+     clearProblem: () => set({ problem: null })
+   }
+ })
+ 
+ export const voiceAgents = agentsHere
+

step.text:
Now I'm setting up the orb as the main visual centerpiece. I'm defining an interface that tracks the orb's state—the smoothed audio band levels, overall intensity, radius expansion, harmonic wobble, rotation, and glow intensity.

The shape itself uses harmonic decomposition: the radius at any angle is the base radius multiplied by a sum of sine waves, where each harmonic is driven by a different frequency band. Lower bands create slow, large swells while higher bands produce fine ripples. Each harmonic rotates at its own rate to create the turning motion. At rest, it breathes gently with just one slow harmonic.

I'm designing it with 5 bands matching the color palette, using harmonics k=2 through 6 (skipping k=1 to avoid just translating the circle), with amplitudes weighted so higher frequencies ripple less. The swell expands based on the overall level. I need a reader function that takes the analyser node's frequency data and groups it into those 5 log-spaced bands, then I'll handle three modes: listening shows the mark's own color breathing quietly, hearing reacts to voice in white, and thinking displays the mesh slowly turning without audio response.

For the canvas drawing, I'll clear the frame, build the outline from samples, then fill it either as a solid white bead with a radial gradient for the listening mode, or as 5 colored radial gradients clipped to the path for the mesh mode. I'll add rim lighting on top and an outer glow using the same path.

For the drifting mesh blobs inside the orb, I'm pulling the colors from `MESH_COLORS` but defining the blob positions locally in `orb.ts` with their own drift parameters and animation rates.

Defining the orb blob interface... I'm splitting this into three focused modules: a pure math layer for the orb calculations, a canvas drawing layer, and a React component that ties them together. For the audio analysis, I'm defining a function that takes a spectrum array and sample rate to extract frequency bands across the voice range, computing which bins fall into each of five log-spaced bands from 60Hz to 6kHz.

Writing the band extraction logic... Writing step function...
Now the orb, split the way the games and boot are: numbers, picture, canvas.

+ import { MESH_COLORS } from '../CrewMark'
+ 
+ // The shape of the orb, as numbers. Nothing here draws anything or knows what a
+ // canvas is, the same split the games hold.
+ //
+ // A circle that only changes size is a circle changing size. What makes one of
+ // these read as a voice is that the edge itself moves, and moves differently at
+ // different parts of it: the bass swells one side of the whole shape, and a
+ // sibilant ripples the rim. So the outline is a circle with a harmonic on it
+ // per band of what is being heard, low bands on the slow harmonics and high
+ // bands on the fast ones.
+ 
+ export const BANDS = 5
+ 
+ // Never the first harmonic. One lobe around a circle is the circle moved
+ // sideways, so the orb would slide about the screen rather than breathe.
+ export const HARMONICS = [2, 3, 5, 7, 9]
+ 
+ // How much each harmonic is allowed to bend the edge. High frequencies are
+ // quick and everywhere, so left equal they turn the orb into a gear.
+ const WEIGHT = [0.115, 0.085, 0.055, 0.038, 0.026]
+ 
+ // How fast each harmonic turns, and how much louder makes it hurry.
+ const SPIN = [0.32, -0.24, 0.19, -0.15, 0.12]
+ const SPIN_GAIN = 1.5
+ 
+ const LOW_HZ = 70
+ const HIGH_HZ = 6000
+ 
+ const RISE_TAU = 0.028
+ const FALL_TAU = 0.19
+ const LIT_TAU = 0.22
+ const RING_TAU = 0.3
+ 
+ const BREATH_RATE = 0.55
+ const REST_SWELL = 0.017
+ const SWELL = 0.17
+ 
+ // The mark's own mesh, arranged in a disc rather than across a wordmark. The
+ // colors are not this file's to choose: the app says anything it says in color
+ // through that one palette.
+ export interface OrbBlob {
+   color: string
+   x: number
+   y: number
+   r: number
+   reach: number
+   rate: number
+   lag: number
+ }
+ 
+ const PLACES = [
+   { x: -0.34, y: -0.3, r: 0.86, reach: 0.16, rate: 0.41, lag: 0 },
+   { x: 0.31, y: -0.16, r: 0.8, reach: 0.19, rate: -0.33, lag: 1.7 },
+   { x: 0.12, y: 0.38, r: 0.9, reach: 0.15, rate: 0.27, lag: 3.1 },
+   { x: -0.28, y: 0.34, r: 0.74, reach: 0.21, rate: -0.45, lag: 4.6 },
+   { x: 0.02, y: -0.06, r: 0.5, reach: 0.24, rate: 0.53, lag: 2.2 }
+ ]
+ 
+ export const ORB_BLOBS: OrbBlob[] = MESH_COLORS.map((color, index) => ({ color, ...PLACES[index % PLACES.length] }))
+ 
+ export interface OrbFace {
+   bands: number[]
+   phases: number[]
+   level: number
+   swell: number
+   breath: number
+   // How far the mesh has come up. It is the agent's voice that lights the orb:
+   // your own turn leaves it in the one color the mark wears at rest.
+   lit: number
+   ring: number
+ }
+ 
+ export const restingOrb = (): OrbFace => ({
+   bands: new Array(BANDS).fill(0),
+   phases: HARMONICS.map((_, index) => index * 1.7),
+   level: 0,
+   swell: 1,
+   breath: 0,
+   lit: 0,
+   ring: 0
+ })
+ 
+ const bandOf = (hz: number): number => {
+   const share = Math.log(Math.max(LOW_HZ, Math.min(HIGH_HZ, hz)) / LOW_HZ) / Math.log(HIGH_HZ / LOW_HZ)
+   return Math.min(BANDS - 1, Math.max(0, Math.floor(share * BANDS)))
+ }
+ 
+ // A spectrum as the few numbers the shape is made of. Byte data rather than
+ // float, because the shape only needs to know loud from quiet.
+ export function bandsFrom(spectrum: Uint8Array, sampleRate: number, into: number[]): number {
+   const width = sampleRate / 2 / spectrum.length
+   const sums = new Array(BANDS).fill(0)
+   const counts = new Array(BANDS).fill(0)
+   for (let bin = 1; bin < spectrum.length; bin++) {
+     const band = bandOf((bin + 0.5) * width)
+     sums[band] += spectrum[bin]
+     counts[band]++
+   }
+   let total = 0
+   for (let band = 0; band < BANDS; band++) {
+     into[band] = counts[band] > 0 ? Math.min(1, sums[band] / counts[band] / 190) : 0
+     total += into[band]
+   }
+   return total / BANDS
+ }
+ 
+ const toward = (held: number, want: number, dt: number, tau: number): number =>
+   held + (want - held) * (1 - Math.exp(-dt / Math.max(1e-4, tau)))
+ 
+ export function stepOrb(face: OrbFace, dt: number, read: readonly number[], lit: number, ring: number): void {
+   let total = 0
+   for (let band = 0; band < BANDS; band++) {
+     const want = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, read[band] ?? 0))
+     // Up on the instant and down over a breath, so a syllable reads as a hit
+     // rather than as a wave, which is the same rule the music's bars follow.
+     face.bands[band] = toward(face.bands[band], want, dt, want > face.bands[band] ? RISE_TAU : FALL_TAU)
+     face.phases[band] += (SPIN[band] + face.bands[band] * SPIN_GAIN * Math.sign(SPIN[band])) * dt
+     total += face.bands[band]
+   }
+   face.level = total / BANDS
+   face.breath += dt * BREATH_RATE
+   face.lit = toward(face.lit, lit, dt, LIT_TAU)
+   face.ring = toward(face.ring, ring, dt, RING_TAU)
+   face.swell = 1 + face.level * SWELL + Math.sin(face.breath) * REST_SWELL
+ }
+ 
+ // The edge of the orb, at one angle. Read all the way round it, this is the
+ // outline; the harmonics are what make it a voice rather than a balloon.
+ export function orbRadius(face: OrbFace, angle: number, base: number): number {
+   let bend = 0
+   for (let band = 0; band < BANDS; band++) {
+     bend += Math.sin(HARMONICS[band] * angle + face.phases[band]) * WEIGHT[band] * face.bands[band]
+   }
+   return base * face.swell * (1 + bend)
+ }
+

- ## Huddles
- 
+ ## Toasts
+ 
+ A word from the app about what just happened, standing under the header on the right for a few seconds. `toast()` in `src/renderer/src/state/toast.ts` raises one from anywhere, in the renderer or out of a handler, and `Toaster` is the one stack, mounted once in `App` and standing in the body.
+ 
+ - It is for a moment, never for a record. Anything somebody has to come back to belongs in the chat, in a thread, or on the row it is about, and a toast that says what a screen already says is a row of type spent on nothing.
+ - The tones are plain, done, fail and busy, and each one brings its own mark: nothing, the check, the warning, the spinner. A busy one waits rather than running out, and the handle it hands back turns it over: `toast.busy('Sharing the session').done('Link copied')` is one row saying two things rather than two rows.
+ - `key` is one row per thing. Asked for again under the same key it is rewritten where it stands, so the same word said twice is said once. Four rows is the whole stack, and the oldest goes when a fifth arrives.
+ - The row itself is the way out, and a button on it is the button's own. Nothing runs out while it is being read: the pointer resting anywhere on the stack holds every clock in it.
+ - The card wears `glass glass-strong`, the same material as anything else that floats over whatever the app happens to be showing. It says its own `--glass-shadow` rather than the popover's: a popover is one card and throws a drop deeper than the gap between rows, so four of them pool into one dark box standing behind the stack.
+ - A row opens and closes on its own `grid-template-rows`, which is the one way a box as tall as its text can be animated, and nothing anywhere clips: a box that clips its card clips the shadow with it, and the card reads as standing in a hole. The card keeps its height the whole way out and the fade is what carries it off.
+ - The server has a word of its own for this, `notice`, which goes to the one socket it is about and is never written down. It is what says why a command did not happen, so nobody else scrolls past an answer to a question they never asked.
+

+ import { orbRadius, ORB_BLOBS, type OrbFace } from './orb'
+ 
+ // How many points the outline is read at. Fewer and the harmonics come out as a
+ // polygon; the highest one turns nine times around the circle, so it needs
+ // several points per lobe before it is a curve at all.
+ const STEPS = 180
+ 
+ const RING_WIDTH = 2
+ 
+ export interface OrbPaint {
+   // What the orb is drawn in when the mesh is down, which is whatever the app
+   // is set in. The mark is currentColor at rest and so is this.
+   ink: string
+   ring: string

+ const around = (face: OrbFace, base: number, at: number): { x: number; y: number } => {
+   const angle = (at / STEPS) * Math.PI * 2
+   const radius = orbRadius(face, angle, base)
+   return { x: Math.cos(angle) * radius, y: Math.sin(angle) * radius }
+ }
+ 
+ // A closed curve through the points rather than a line to each one. Straight
+ // segments show up as facets the moment the orb is still, which is most of the
+ // time it is on screen.
+ function outline(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, face: OrbFace, base: number): void {
+   ctx.beginPath()
+   const first = around(face, base, 0)
+   const last = around(face, base, STEPS - 1)
+   ctx.moveTo((last.x + first.x) / 2, (last.y + first.y) / 2)
+   for (let at = 0; at < STEPS; at++) {
+     const here = around(face, base, at)
+     const next = around(face, base, at + 1)
+     ctx.quadraticCurveTo(here.x, here.y, (here.x + next.x) / 2, (here.y + next.y) / 2)
+   }
+   ctx.closePath()
+ }
+ 
+ export function drawOrb(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   face: OrbFace,
+   size: number,
+   base: number,
+   paint: OrbPaint

+   ctx.clearRect(0, 0, size, size)
+   ctx.save()
+   ctx.translate(half, half)

+   // The light the orb throws, drawn first and wide. It is the same field the
+   // inside is, so what spills is the color of what is behind the glass.

+   glow.addColorStop(1, withAlpha(paint.ink, 0))

+   ctx.fillRect(-half, -half, size, size)
+ 
+   outline(ctx, face, base)
+   ctx.save()
+   ctx.clip()
+ 
+   const body = ctx.createRadialGradient(-base * 0.3, -base * 0.34, base * 0.05, 0, 0, base * 1.25)

+   body.addColorStop(0.55, withAlpha(paint.ink, 0.82))
+   body.addColorStop(1, withAlpha(paint.ink, 0.6))
+   ctx.fillStyle = body
+   ctx.fillRect(-half, -half, size, size)
+ 
+   // The mesh, only as far up as the agent's own voice has brought it. Painted
+   // over the body rather than instead of it, so the two ends of the fade are
+   // the same drawing at two strengths.

+     ctx.globalAlpha = face.lit
+     ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'source-over'

+       const blob = ORB_BLOBS[index]
+       const turn = face.breath * blob.rate + blob.lag
+       const push = blob.reach * (0.6 + face.bands[index % face.bands.length] * 1.6)

+       const y = (blob.y + Math.sin(turn * 0.86) * push) * base
+       const r = blob.r * base * (1 + face.bands[index % face.bands.length] * 0.22)

+       wash.addColorStop(0, withAlpha(blob.color, 0.95))
+       wash.addColorStop(0.45, withAlpha(blob.color, 0.6))
+       wash.addColorStop(1, withAlpha(blob.color, 0))
+       ctx.fillStyle = wash
+       ctx.fillRect(-half, -half, size, size)
+     }
+     ctx.globalAlpha = 1
+   }
+ 
+   // Where the light lands, and the shade drawn in all round the edge. Between
+   // them they are the difference between a disc and a bead, which is the same
+   // pair of passes the app icon's discs are built from.
+   const shine = ctx.createRadialGradient(-base * 0.36, -base * 0.42, 0, -base * 0.36, -base * 0.42, base * 0.95)
+   shine.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(255,255,255,0.42)')
+   shine.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(255,255,255,0)')
+   ctx.fillStyle = shine
+   ctx.fillRect(-half, -half, size, size)
+ 
+   const shade = ctx.createRadialGradient(0, 0, base * 0.62, 0, 0, base * 1.02)

+   const radius = base * 1.22
+   ctx.lineWidth = RING_WIDTH

+   ctx.strokeStyle = withAlpha(color, 0.16)
+   ctx.beginPath()
+   ctx.arc(0, 0, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2)
+   ctx.stroke()
+   ctx.strokeStyle = withAlpha(color, 0.9)
+   ctx.beginPath()
+   ctx.arc(0, 0, radius, -Math.PI / 2, -Math.PI / 2 + Math.PI * 2 * at)
+   ctx.stroke()
+ }

+ // A color the app already holds, at an opacity. The app's own are given as

+ export function withAlpha(color: string, alpha: number): string {
+   const hex = /^#([0-9a-f]{3}|[0-9a-f]{6})$/i.exec(color.trim())
+   if (hex) {
+     const raw = hex[1]
+     const full = raw.length === 3 ? [...raw].map(one => one + one).join('') : raw
+     const value = parseInt(full, 16)
+     return `rgba(${(value >> 16) & 255}, ${(value >> 8) & 255}, ${value & 255}, ${alpha})`
+   }
+   const parts = /^rgba?\(([^)]+)\)$/i.exec(color.trim())
+   if (parts) {
+     const [r, g, b] = parts[1].split(/[\s,/]+/).filter(Boolean)
+     return `rgba(${r}, ${g}, ${b}, ${alpha})`
+   }
+   return color
+ }

I need to add toast notifications whenever a desktop notification would have been triggered. Looking at the `finishedAlert` function, I see that notifications only fire when the window isn't focused — so I should mirror that logic and show toasts in those same cases, rather than duplicating notifications when the user is already viewing the app.

The key insight is that toasts should be the in-app equivalent of OS notifications: when an agent finishes, I'll show a toast with the agent's mark and an action button to open that thread. This gives users the same notification experience whether they're in the app or away from it.

For timing, I'm thinking about pausing toast countdowns while the window is unfocused — nothing should disappear while nobody's watching. Instead of a single `held` boolean, I could track holds as a set of reasons like 'pointer' and 'away', so window blur adds 'away' and focus removes it. That way multiple hold conditions can coexist cleanly.

The feature only works if toasts stick around when you're away, since notifications fire while you're gone. If the toast burns down before you return, the whole thing fails. So I need to implement this.

Now I'm checking how the notification click handler opens a thread in App.tsx so the toast action can mirror that behavior.

The issue is that `agentsHere(member.id)` filters agents by ownership, so when the runner connects as 'jamel' but the UI is 'sam', the query returns nothing since the test agent belongs to jamel. This is the correct behavior for ghost threads, which can only route to your own agents, though voice agents work differently since they run on the owner's machine.

I need to refactor the taker selection logic to use `agentsHere()` without an owner filter for voice calls, while keeping the ownership check for ghost threads. The code is getting nested, so I'll restructure it for clarity. In the real app the client explicitly specifies the agent anyway, so this unnamed fallback just needs to work correctly.
The unnamed case wrongly required the agent be *yours* (that rule belongs to ghost threads). Fixing:

Jamel wants the built-in toasts to display for every qualifying alert event regardless of whether the user is focused on the app, so I need to remove the focus-based gating. But there's a nuance here — should the toast still appear when the user is already viewing the specific thread that triggered the alert? The current logic returns null from `finishedAlert` when both watching and the open thread ID match, which suggests we might want to suppress it in that case. Actually, I think the cleaner approach is to just not show a toast for events happening in the current view—whether that's the thread you're reading or the main chat. So the mention toast fires unless the message is in the thread or chat you're actively looking at, and the same logic applies to run completions. That way I'm not overthinking the focus state; the rule is simply about what's already visible on your screen. I'm leaning toward the simpler rule: toast everything except what's happening in the view you're currently on. That avoids redundancy—a finished run already shows in the thread's status, and a mention appears right there in the chat you're reading—while still respecting the "always show toasts" intent by dropping the focus check entirely. I'll lay this out clearly so Jamel can push back if the "same view" exclusion isn't what they meant.

For the implementation, I'm adding optional fields to the alert type to track which agent and person are involved, plus a flag for stopped runs so they get the warning styling and longer display time—those deserve attention. The pet identifier still matters even for failures since it tells you which agent to look at.

Then I need to be careful with the alert functions: I'm changing them to check whether you're viewing the relevant surface rather than just whether the app is focused, so one alert can work across both places. But I have to preserve the OS notification behavior—it shouldn't fire while the app is in focus, which is the current standard for mentions.

So the solution is to separate the concerns: build the alert using the "not the view you're on" rule, always show the toast, but gate the OS notification to only fire when the window isn't focused. That means `showAlert` in main only runs if `!document.hasFocus()`. This is actually a slight behavior change—currently the OS notification fires even when focused but on another thread, but removing that makes sense since the toast is already visible to you.

Now I'm restructuring the code to handle this cleanly. I'll create a single `alertFor` function that takes the event and state, returning either an alert or null, then use that to decide whether to show the toast and OS notification based on focus state.

For the toast rendering, I need a separate module that converts an AgentAlert into a React node since the toast function accepts ReactNode marks — I'm thinking `src/renderer/src/state/alertToast.tsx` to keep it colocated with the alert logic while having access to React components.

Then when a toast is triggered, it'll call `useCrew.getState().openThread(threadId)` to open the thread, and the App component will have an effect that switches to the chat tab when that happens.

The tests are passing so far. Now I need to tackle the mouth test, which covers the most complex real-time behavior — streaming playback and barge-in using FakeAudio and a fake Worker. I'm checking what FakeAudio's buffer source supports: it has `start`, `stop`, and `connect` methods, but it doesn't fire the `onended` event that the mouth relies on to detect when playback finishes. I'll need to extend the test to handle firing those events manually.

Rather than modifying the shared FakeAudio helper that other tests depend on, I'll create a local fake tailored to the mouth test that tracks scheduled sources and lets the test end them. The AudioContext gets memoized at module scope in audio.ts, so it persists across tests in the same file, which is fine. Each test file has its own module registry in vitest anyway.

Writing the voice-mouth test file now — I'll stub AudioContext to record buffer sources, stub Worker to echo open/push/close messages as said/done events, then drive VoiceMouth through its lifecycle: open, push two sentences, seal, verify the buffers schedule back-to-back with captions in order and onQuiet firing after both end. I'll also test stopping mid-playback to ensure nothing else schedules and onQuiet fires once.

For the Worker fake, I need to capture the instance so the test can control it — the fake will store itself on a static property and provide a reply method to send messages back. The audio fake needs createBufferSource to return an object where I can trigger onended callbacks. For timing, mouth.play uses setTimeout for captions, and with currentTime at 100 and a 0.06 second lead time, the timeout calculation works out naturally.

I'll use vi.useFakeTimers to control the timing in tests, setting the fake's currentTime and advancing the timers as needed.

I'm sketching out the alert state structure with an interface that extends ReviewState to include agent information and a thread ID, then defining a function to determine when an alert should be triggered based on session events.

Refining the guard logic: I need to check if the event has a threadId and whether it matches the currently open thread, skipping the alert only in that case. The original condition was too broad—it would incorrectly suppress alerts for main chat runs. Simplifying to just compare threadIds directly without the `watching` flag, and applying the same pattern to the mention alert function.

For the mention case, there's a subtle issue: when `threadId` is undefined (main chat message) and `openThreadId` is null (viewing main chat), the condition correctly skips the alert since you're already reading it. But if you're on the Docs tab with `openThreadId` still null, a mention in the main chat would still toast, which is a bit redundant. The tradeoff is keeping the logic simple and symmetric—only suppress when you're actively viewing that specific thread—versus adding tab tracking to the store, which adds complexity.

Jamel's preference leans toward showing toasts more often rather than suppressing them, so I'll go with the minimal exclusion: skip only when you have that exact thread open, and let main chat mentions always toast even if they're visible on screen. It mirrors Slack's behavior of not toasting when you're in the channel, but errs on the side of what they asked for.

The tricky part is that the store doesn't track which tab you're on—it only knows if a thread is open. So if you switch from a thread to the Docs tab, the openThreadId stays set, which means a message finishing in that thread wouldn't toast even though you're not actually viewing it anymore. That's a gap, but it's probably acceptable given the constraints.

Rather than adding tab state to the store (which feels like over-engineering), I'll stick with the minimal fix: keep the existing check for `event.threadId && openThreadId === event.threadId`, always toast main-chat messages, and accept that the Docs-tab edge case matches the current behavior. It's the smallest change and doesn't require refactoring the store.

The mention alert currently gates on `watching` to prevent toasts while focused, but removing that means every @mention will toast—which is exactly what's being asked for. I'm working through a CSS selector issue with AgentIcon inside a toast component. The toast slot applies `[&>svg]:w-[18px]` to force SVG children to 18px, but since AgentIcon wraps its SVG in a span, that selector doesn't match the nested SVG—so the outer span stays at 20px while the inner SVG gets constrained, causing a mismatch.

The cleanest fix is to resize the toast's mark slot itself to 20px (matching AgentIcon's xs size) while keeping the inner SVG at 18px, which preserves the glyph appearance and lets Avatar or AgentIcon fill the slot properly. Since Avatar and AgentIcon both read from Zustand hooks, they need to be rendered elements in the toast, which they already are.

For wiring this into the store, `alertToast` needs to live in a `.tsx` file since it uses JSX, while `store.ts` imports it and passes a callback like `threadId => get().openThread(threadId)` to avoid tight coupling. There's a potential circular dependency since AgentIcon imports the store and the store imports alertToast, but as long as nothing executes at module initialization, ESM handles it fine. I could pass the agent data (id and name) through the toast options instead of building the ReactNode in the store, which would let the Toaster component handle rendering the face. That keeps the store decoupled from UI concerns and avoids the circular dependency, though it does add crew-specific fields to the toast API. - ## The menu bar
+ ## Voice
+ 
+ Talking to an agent out loud, back and forth. It is a tile in the toolbox and `/voice` in the chat, and it opens a screen of its own with the orb on it. Everything that listens and everything that speaks runs on this machine and costs nothing: whisper for the ear, kokoro for the mouth, both fetched once from their own model repositories and kept by the browser after that. There is no service behind it and nothing said in a conversation leaves the machine except the words themselves, which go to the agent the way a typed message does.
+ 
+ - A conversation is an ordinary thread. What was said goes in the chat, the agent does real work on real files, and the crew reads it afterwards, so voice is a way into a thread rather than a room beside one. The thread wears `voice`, and the host adds `VOICE_INSTRUCTIONS` to every prompt in it exactly the way plan mode adds its own. Nothing about the brief is ever a message, so the chat holds what people said and not what the app told the agent.
+ - That brief is the whole of what makes a spoken answer sound spoken. Without it a model writes three paragraphs of markdown, and a voice reads out every asterisk in them. It asks for a sentence or two in plain words, and it is what teaches the agent to draw a card.
+ - Both models run in workers of their own. A turn of whisper is a second of solid arithmetic, and a second of that on the thread drawing the orb is a second of the orb standing still. Nothing heavy is imported anywhere but those two files, which is what keeps the runtime and its wasm out of the app's own bundle.
+ - The microphone stays open the whole time, the agent's turn included, and `echoCancellation` is what makes that possible. While the agent is speaking the gate asks for more before it believes it has been interrupted, or the agent talks itself to a stop.
+ - Cutting in stops the voice and nothing else. Whatever the agent is doing to the project it goes on doing, because an interruption is somebody talking over an answer and not somebody undoing work. What the model had already drawn and not yet played is dropped rather than let out afterwards.
+ - `VoiceGate` is where one thing somebody said starts and ends. A level alone cannot answer that, so it tracks the floor the room is sitting at and opens on whatever stands well above it for long enough. The floor only moves while nobody is talking: tracked through an utterance it climbs into the voice and closes the gate mid-sentence. A click is one frame and never opens it, a cough opens it and is dropped for being too short, and a microphone somebody left open lets go on its own.
+ - Every sample is kept, through an `AudioWorklet`. An analyser hands back the last window it holds and nothing about the gaps between reads, which is fine for a ring around whoever is talking and useless for keeping the words. The few hundred milliseconds before the gate opened are kept too, or every utterance is missing the front of its first word and whisper guesses at it.
+ - The answer is spoken while it is still being written, and two things stop that being a plain hand-off of whatever just landed. A sentence is the smallest thing worth saying, so a part one is held back. And nothing past an unclosed fence is ever handed over, so a card is either whole or not there: `VoiceReply` is both of those, and the line it stops on can never fall inside a card, because a line ending inside one is still a line ending and the front of a card read out loud is a line of JSON.
+ - A card is the thing worth looking at rather than hearing. `VoiceCard` in `src/shared/voice.ts` is the whole of what one may be, five kinds and no more, and one with nothing on it comes back as null rather than as an empty box beside the orb. They arrive as the agent writes them rather than at the end, and the options on a choice are answered by tapping one, which goes in as a turn of its own so it reads back the way saying it would have.
+ - The orb is drawn the way the games are: `orb.ts` holds the numbers, `drawOrb.ts` holds the picture, and neither knows about the other. It is read off a real analyser hung on whichever of the two is making sound, never off a shape standing in for one.
+ - A circle that only changes size is a circle changing size. What makes one of these read as a voice is that the edge itself moves, and differently at different parts of it, so the outline carries a harmonic per band of what is being heard, low bands on the slow harmonics and high on the fast. Never the first harmonic: one lobe around a circle is the circle moved sideways, and the orb would wander about the screen while it talked.
+ - The mesh is the agent's voice and nothing else. Your own turn leaves the orb in the one color the mark wears at rest, so who is talking is read off it without a word anywhere saying so, and the colors are the mark's own `MESH_COLORS` rather than a palette this invents.
+ - The renderer's CSP has to carry `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' blob:` and `worker-src 'self' blob:`, or the worklet never loads and the runtime never compiles. Both fail quietly and both look like a microphone that does nothing.
+ - `tests/voice-listening.test.ts` holds the gate to all of the above, `tests/voice-reply.test.ts` feeds a reply in one character at a time and holds it to saying every word once and never a line of a card, and `tests/voice-mouth.test.ts` runs the speaker against a clock it winds by hand.

The test failure in `tests/thread-view-probe.test.ts` was already present before my changes—it's from another agent's work on the `openThreadId` and boot flow. I'm cleaning up the worktree and doing a final review of my code to catch any real bugs before wrapping up.

Looking at the audio handling logic, I've spotted a correctness issue: when an utterance gets dropped, I clear the session state but never signal back to the session that we've returned to listening. If a cough interrupts speech, the orb would get stuck in the 'hearing' state. I need to add a way for the ear to notify the session when a dropped utterance occurs—either by adding an `onDrop` callback or by changing `onEnd` to accept `null` when there's no actual audio to process.

In the voice state, there's a potential issue with overlapping utterances: if the user starts talking again while the whisper API is still processing the first one, both messages get sent and the reply tracking for the first gets overwritten. The first reply ends up orphaned since `promptId` resets on each send, which is actually the right behavior—the user changed their mind. The mouth opening per send bumps the turn counter and stops playback of the previous response, so that works out.

There's also a performance concern in the watcher: the `findTurn` scan runs on every store change, which is O(events) complexity.  It early-returns once the promptId is found, so it's only a reverse scan of up to 500 events for a couple seconds—acceptable. The `textOf` helper rebuilds the string each time too, but that's a small join operation. The `speak()` helper guards against pushing empty text, and when `mouth.seal()` is called with nothing (like when the reply is only a card), the worker's splitter closes cleanly, the TTS stream yields nothing, and the done signal triggers the quiet handler.

Now I'm thinking through what happens when the TTS stream is empty—the async generator should complete when `close()` is called, but if the model is still loading, `run()` waits for that first, so a card-only reply could leave us stuck in 'thinking' until the model loads. That's only an issue on the first turn though, and we wait for `ready` before opening the mic anyway. But there's a potential hang: after the reply ends, I'm checking `mouth.speaking` to decide whether to switch to 'listening', and `mouth.speaking` depends on whether `drained` is true and `waiting` is zero. After `open()` runs, `drained` gets set to false, so...

Actually, right after sealing the mouth, `speaking` is still true because the worker hasn't sent `done` yet, so we stay in 'thinking' until `onQuiet` fires. If the worker never sends `done` for some reason, we'd be stuck in 'thinking' forever, but the gate still works—`onStart` fires and moves us to 'hearing', so the user can talk again and recover. The `onQuiet` handler only transitions to 'listening' if we're currently in 'speaking', but if the reply was card-only or empty, we never actually entered 'speaking' in the first place.

That's a real bug: `onQuiet` fires while we're still in 'thinking' and nothing changes. The fix is to let `onQuiet` transition to 'listening' from either 'speaking' or 'thinking'. I need to be careful about the order of operations during barge-in though—when `stop()` fires `onQuiet`, the phase is still 'speaking', so it sets 'listening', then we immediately set 'hearing'. But if I broaden `onQuiet` to handle 'thinking' as well, I need to trace through what happens in `answer()` when we call `mouth.stop()` followed by `send()`. Broadening the condition is safe, so I'll go with it. There's an edge case where the agent's reply is empty and there are no cards—nothing gets spoken and the conversation goes silent, but I'll leave that as-is since onQuiet will transition to listening. For muting, setting `track.enabled = false` silences the worklet and keeps the gate closed. The issue I'm spotting now is in the `VoiceEar.open()` failure path—if opening the ear fails, I set the problem flag but the phase stays stuck in 'waking' because `woke()` requires ready to equal 2.

The tricky part is that the models might still load and flip to 'listening' even though the mic is dead, which would be misleading. Rather than adding a separate flag, I can set phase to 'listening' but display the problem message on screen instead of the caption—this way the error text shows ("crew could not reach your microphone") and the controls remain functional, which feels like enough feedback without getting tangled in phase logic.

Now I'm thinking through the `stepOrb` function with reduced motion enabled. When `dt = 0`, the exponential smoothing formula collapses to just returning the current value, so the orb bands never animate at all. My test confirms this behavior, but I'm questioning whether completely freezing the orb is the right call—reduced motion should suppress decorative animation, not eliminate functional feedback about who's talking.

Looking at the precedent in AGENTS.md, landing the mark where it is aligns with standing things down under reduced motion, so keeping the orb still is consistent with the app's philosophy. The caption updates still provide state feedback, which is acceptable. I could make the orb respond to voice while suppressing idle breathing and spin, but that feels like splitting hairs when users enable reduced motion specifically to stop pulsing elements like this. I'll stick with the current approach and leave the test as written.

There's another issue though—with `dt = 0`, the `face.ring` animation also never advances, which I need to check.

Refactoring the approach: instead of killing all motion, I should stop only the *phases* and *breath* while letting level tracking continue. I'm adding a `still` flag to the stepOrb function that lets the bands track voice input, the lit state and ring progress update normally, but the decorative animations freeze. This way the orb still responds gently to voice through size changes without the idle motion. Implementing the stepOrb function...

Now I'm noticing a real issue with the NOTHING regex in the listen worker — it's filtering out responses like "okay" and "so" that are actually meaningful answers to questions, not just hallucinations. If someone says "okay" in response to "shall I run it?", that should register, not get dropped. The current pattern is too aggressive and creates a UX bug where valid user responses disappear.

I need to be more surgical about this. Whisper typically hallucinates things like "Thank you", "you", "Bye", or bracketed sounds on silence — those are the real artifacts. But "yeah", "okay", "um", "uh" are things people genuinely say, so I should remove those from the filter. The `worthSending` check already handles single characters and non-alphanumeric content anyway, so I can trim the NOTHING list down to just the actual hallucination patterns.

For the voice state management, I'm noticing that `end()` deliberately doesn't close the mouth or listener workers — it keeps them loaded so the next conversation starts instantly. The mic track does get closed though. And `ready` gets reset when `start()` is called again, which triggers the workers to reload. The memoized promise just re-resolves, so there's no actual duplication happening.

I need to trace where the composer's keyboard handling comes from and look at how the tokenizer works in `emojiTokens.ts`. The core approach is treating the composer as a textarea with a highlight overlay that renders the same text but with styled mentions and emojis. For markdown support, I'd render the formatting markers dimly while showing the styled text—so `**bold**` appears bold with the asterisks faded, `__underline__` shows underlined text, and `*italic*` renders italicized.

But there's a fundamental problem: if the overlay applies bold or italic styling, those fonts are wider or have different metrics than the base font, which means the text wraps differently and the caret position drifts out of sync with what the textarea actually renders. Other apps like Slack and Discord sidestep this by using contenteditable instead. The workaround here is to only apply styles that preserve metrics—color, opacity, underline, strikethrough, background washes—and avoid bold and italic, or find a monospace font where those variants have identical widths. I could use `-webkit-text-stroke` to fake bold without changing glyph widths — that's a genuinely metric-safe approach. Italic is trickier since `font-style: italic` uses a different face with different metrics, and `transform: skewX()` doesn't work on inline elements. But looking back at what was actually asked for — bold, underline, bullets — maybe italic isn't even required here.

Actually, I'm realizing the real focus might be less about rendering rich text in the composer and more about making markdown authoring comfortable: keyboard shortcuts like ⌘B for `**`, ⌘I for `*`, ⌘U for `__`, plus list handling where Enter continues the list and Tab indents items. There's also smart paste behavior where dropping a URL over selected text wraps it as a link, and the overlay dims the markdown markers so the text reads cleanly. Jamel wants the composer to support Discord-style markdown, where the syntax characters remain visible but the enclosed text gets styled—so `**bold**` shows both asterisks and renders the text in bold, with the asterisks staying visible in the same color as the surrounding text. Discord supports bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, inline code with background, code blocks, blockquotes, headers, and lists (with list markers highlighted but not converted to bullet glyphs). The keyboard shortcuts are Ctrl/Cmd+B for bold, Ctrl/Cmd+I for italic, Ctrl/Cmd+U for underline, and Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+X for strikethrough. I'm trying to recall the exact shortcuts for code formatting and whether Discord auto-continues lists when you press Shift+Enter after typing a list marker. I'm also wondering if selecting text and pressing a markdown character wraps the selection automatically. The core technical challenge is that Discord uses a contenteditable element with real formatting, whereas a transparent textarea overlay can't change glyph metrics without the caret position drifting out of sync. Converting to contenteditable would solve this but introduces significant complexity around mentions and emoji handling. Option B explores keeping the textarea while using CSS tricks like `-webkit-text-stroke` for bold to maintain consistent character widths, though italic presents its own challenge. System fonts like SF Pro have actual italic faces with different metrics, so even using `font-style: oblique` won't fully solve the problem—the caret drawn by the textarea will still drift relative to the overlay if the styled text has different advance widths. For a truly robust solution, I need to keep metrics identical. For bold, I can use `-webkit-text-stroke` to thicken the outline without reflowing. For italic, `transform: skewX()` requires `display: inline-block` which breaks word wrapping inside the run, so that won't work for italic text containing spaces that needs to wrap across lines. The real issue is that the textarea and overlay will always have inherent mismatches. The better approach is what Discord does: use a contenteditable with a flat text structure and apply markdown styling as pure decorations on top, keeping the underlying document as plain text for serialization. But contenteditable brings its own headaches—composition events, Android quirks, undo stack management, paste handling. I need to weigh the scope here: touching the composer would ripple through Chat, ThreadView, DesignChat, plus all the hooks and utilities around selection, mentions, slash commands, and the various test suites. That's a lot of surface area for a rewrite, and the project emphasizes integration tests and full coverage. Let me think about a hybrid approach instead—keep the textarea but style the overlay to match its exact font metrics. Bold could use text-stroke, but italic is trickier. Or flip it entirely: make the textarea text visible and have the overlay only handle backgrounds and underlines, skipping bold styling altogether. Discord does something similar, so maybe that's the direction to explore. Actually, contenteditable might be the better path here. Since Jamel wants something as robust as Discord's solution, a from-scratch contenteditable is risky with all the IME, undo, and browser quirks—though Electron being Chromium-only does simplify things. Using `contenteditable="plaintext-only"` gives native undo/redo, IME support, proper caret and selection, and automatic plain-text-only pasting, while still allowing styled child spans. The tricky part is that the browser mutates the DOM directly when typing, which fights React's re-rendering. The standard approach (used by CodeMirror, ProseMirror, and Slate) is to let the browser edit, then read the text back via `onBeforeInput` or `onInput`, save the caret position, trigger a re-render, and restore the selection afterward. For a single-line plain-text field, this machinery is manageable—just read `innerText`, compute the caret offset using Range APIs, call onChange, then walk the text nodes to restore the caret on the next render. The challenge is handling newlines correctly with `innerText`—whether to use `
` elements or `white-space: pre-wrap` with actual newline characters—and dealing with quirks like trailing newlines needing a trailing `
`. This is a high-risk change since the input field is the most-used control in the app and is shared across three views plus the mention/slash autocomplete that rely on `selectionStart`. There's a real tension between matching Discord exactly and maintaining robustness—a hand-rolled contenteditable is actually less reliable than a textarea in practice, even if it looks better. But wait, I'm reconsidering the metrics problem. If I can make the overlay layout match the textarea exactly, I get Discord's visual style with textarea's robustness—that's genuinely the best solution. The textarea controls wrapping and caret position, so the overlay needs to produce identical layout. I can't apply per-range styling directly to the textarea, but what if I use `text-shadow` to simulate bold without changing character widths? That's the classic faux-bold technique—`text-shadow: 0.5px 0 0 currentColor`—which preserves metrics perfectly. For italics, using real `font-style: italic` introduces metric drift since italic fonts have different widths, and over a 20-character run that could shift the caret position noticeably. So I'm exploring an alternative: splitting italic runs into individual words as inline-block elements, each with a `skewX` transform to create the slant effect. Since each word is its own inline-block with its natural width (matching the textarea's metrics), and spaces remain as regular text nodes between them, wrapping should work normally at word boundaries. The skew transformation shifts pixels horizontally without changing the actual width measurement. There's a visual concern though — skewing around the center means the top shifts right and the bottom left, which could cause the bottom-left pixels to slightly overlap the previous character, but that's exactly what italic looks like. The overlay's `overflow: hidden` should handle any clipping at its boundaries. And since inline-blocks default to `vertical-align: baseline`, text alignment should stay consistent. The tricky part is handling long italic words within inline-blocks and how `white-space: pre-wrap` inheritance affects spacing... with a long word in an italic run, the inline-block approach breaks differently than the textarea would. Given how rare that edge case is, I'm leaning toward the simpler solution: faux-bold via text-shadow and per-word skew for italics—it's a hack but pixel-perfect in practice. Discord does render italics slanted in its composer, so I need to match that. I'm settling on a plan: keep the textarea as the actual input, extend the overlay into a full markdown highlighter that shows styled text while keeping the markdown syntax visible, and layer in Discord's editing behaviors—that gets me closest to Discord's feel without the layout fragility of trying to perfectly sync two separate rendering systems. I need to be careful about scope here — changing how `__text__` renders in marked would affect agent output too, since they write markdown and commonly use `__` for bold. If an agent writes `__important__` meaning bold, it'd show as underlined instead, which breaks that expectation. But Jamel specifically asked for Discord-exact behavior, so underline via `__` is what he wants. The visual difference between underline and bold is minor anyway. For spoilers with `||x||`, Discord has them, but they need click-to-reveal functionality in the message renderer — that's a separate feature beyond just markdown highlighting. I'll skip spoilers for now and focus on the core set. So my final composer highlighting will cover bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, code, fenced code blocks, quotes, headings up to level 3, list markers, links, and spoilers, with the syntax characters themselves dimmed like Discord does, and support for nesting like `**bold _and italic_**`. For keyboard shortcuts, I'll implement the standard ones: ⌘B for bold, ⌘I for italics, ⌘U for underline, and ⌘⇧X for strikethrough. I need to be careful with ⌘K since it's already the quick switcher in Crew, so I'll use ⌘K for links instead (the universal convention). For toggle behavior, pressing the shortcut again on formatted text removes the markers, and with no selection it inserts the markers and positions the cursor in the middle. I'm also handling list continuation with Shift+Enter to keep the same list marker. For pasting URLs with selected text, I'll convert it to a markdown link like Discord does. I'm skipping Tab for indentation since the mention menu already uses it. I also need to make sure underscores render as `` tags for underline styling. I should just build this out properly rather than checking in again—Jamel's asked twice, so I'll move forward and look at the CSS styles and theme configuration.
Jamel wants Discord-grade. Let me check the surrounding pieces before I build.

+ const WORDS = ['hear', 'me', 'project']
+ 
+ async function speech(dir) {
+   const file = path.join(dir, 'said.wav')
+   await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
+     const child = spawn('say', ['-o', file, '--data-format=LEF32@16000', SAID], { stdio: 'ignore' })
+     child.on('exit', code => (code === 0 ? resolve() : reject(new Error('say could not make the speech'))))
+     child.on('error', () => reject(new Error('this check needs the say command, which is macOS only')))
+   })
+   const wav = await readFile(file)
+   let at = 12
+   while (at < wav.length - 8) {
+     const id = wav.toString('ascii', at, at + 4)
+     const size = wav.readUInt32LE(at + 4)
+     if (id === 'data') {
+       const raw = wav.subarray(at + 8, at + 8 + size)
+       return new Float32Array(raw.buffer.slice(raw.byteOffset, raw.byteOffset + Math.floor(raw.length / 4) * 4))
+     }
+     at += 8 + size + (size % 2)
+   }
+   throw new Error('the speech came out with nothing in it')
+ }
+ 
+ async function settings(dir) {
+   const file = path.join(dir, 'models.mjs')
+   await build({
+     entryPoints: [path.join(root, 'src/renderer/src/media/voice/models.ts')],
+     bundle: true,
+     format: 'esm',
+     outfile: file,
+     logLevel: 'error'
+   })
+   return import(file)
+ }
+ 
+ const dir = await mkdtemp(path.join(tmpdir(), 'crew-voice-'))
+ try {
+   const [audio, { LISTEN_MODEL, askedOf }] = await Promise.all([speech(dir), settings(dir)])
+   const { env, pipeline } = await import('@huggingface/transformers')
+   env.allowLocalModels = false
+   const listen = await pipeline('automatic-speech-recognition', LISTEN_MODEL, {
+     dtype: { encoder_model: 'q8', decoder_model_merged: 'q8' }
+   })
+   const result = await listen(audio, askedOf(LISTEN_MODEL))
+   const heard = (Array.isArray(result) ? result.map(part => part.text).join(' ') : result.text) ?? ''
+   console.log(`said:  ${SAID}`)
+   console.log(`heard: ${heard.trim()}`)
+   const missed = WORDS.filter(word => !heard.toLowerCase().includes(word))
+   if (missed.length > 0) {
+     console.error(`the listener made nothing of ${missed.join(', ')}`)
+     process.exit(1)
+   }
+   console.log('real speech, the real model, words back out')
+ } catch (error) {
+   console.error(`the listener fell over: ${error.message}`)
+   process.exit(1)
+ } finally {

But that conflicts with the deliberate architectural decision to keep voice at the thread level.

+ import type { SpeakIn, SpeakOut } from '../src/renderer/src/media/voice/speak.worker'
+ 
+ // kokoro's own splitter, held to the one rule that matters here: it is closed
+ // once, and the second close throws. The model is a sentence per push.
+ vi.mock('kokoro-js', () => {
+   class TextSplitterStream {
+     private sentences: string[] = []
+     private closed = false
+     private wake: (() => void) | null = null
+ 
+     push(...parts: string[]): void {
+       if (this.closed) throw new Error('Stream is already closed.')
+       for (const part of parts) if (part.trim()) this.sentences.push(part.trim())
+       this.wake?.()
+       this.wake = null
+     }
+ 
+     close(): void {
+       if (this.closed) throw new Error('Stream is already closed.')
+       this.closed = true
+       this.wake?.()
+       this.wake = null
+     }
+ 
+     async *[Symbol.asyncIterator](): AsyncGenerator<string> {
+       for (;;) {
+         if (this.sentences.length > 0) yield this.sentences.shift()!
+         else if (this.closed) break
+         else await new Promise<void>(resolve => (this.wake = resolve))
+       }
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   class KokoroTTS {
+     static async from_pretrained(): Promise<KokoroTTS> {
+       return new KokoroTTS()
+     }
+     async *stream(stream: TextSplitterStream): AsyncGenerator<{ text: string; audio: { audio: Float32Array } }> {
+       for await (const text of stream) yield { text, audio: { audio: new Float32Array([0.5]) } }
+     }
+   }
+ 
+   return { KokoroTTS, TextSplitterStream }
+ })
+ 
+ const said: SpeakOut[] = []
+ let hear: (message: MessageEvent<SpeakIn>) => void
+ 
+ const say = (message: SpeakIn): void => hear({ data: message } as MessageEvent<SpeakIn>)
+ 
+ // The model answers on a promise chain of its own, so a turn is given a few
+ // passes of the loop to reach the other end before it is read.
+ const settle = async (): Promise<void> => {
+   for (let pass = 0; pass < 12; pass++) await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))
+ }
+ 
+ const spoken = (): string[] => said.filter(out => out.type === 'said').map(out => (out as { text: string }).text)
+

Inside a thread, the `commands` field gets dropped from `chat.send` messages, so voice messages in threads won't carry command data. To add per-message voice support, I'd need to introduce a new voice flag across the protocol layer, server event handling, message storage, and the ChatMessage class—plus restart the host to apply the changes.

But there's a design question here: should I mark voice thread-wide or per-message? Thread-wide is simpler and doesn't touch the protocol, but it means every message in a voice conversation gets a "Spoken" pill, which creates visual repetition that AGENTS.md discourages. Per-message only marks the actually-spoken messages, which in practice is the same visual result for voice conversations but more accurate for typed messages mixed in.

Actually, maybe the answer is to only mark the first message — the one that initiated the thread. That would give a single pill next to the opening timestamp, echoing the Voice chip on the card. But that feels arbitrary; why would only the first message be marked as spoken when all of them were?

I think the most honest approach is to mark each message that was actually spoken, carried on the message itself. Though I'm second-guessing the visual noise — in a back-and-forth conversation, every other row would have the pill, which might feel redundant since the thread card already signals it's a voice conversation.

But Jamel was explicit about wanting it beside the spoken message, and the real value of per-message flagging is handling mixed threads where some parts were spoken and some typed. That's the distinction that matters. So I'll go with carrying the voice flag on each message.

Now I need to wire this through the system: add the voice field to the protocol and events, read it on the server side when processing chat messages, thread it through the store and voice state, and surface it in the components.

The tricky part is sendChat already has six positional parameters, and adding a seventh feels unwieldy. I could either refactor the tail parameters into an options object—which touches a lot of callers—or find a way to reuse the existing commands field, though that conflicts with the stated rule that commands are ignored in threads. Mixed-mode threads are actually real—voice when the screen is open, typing when it's closed in chat—so I'll stick with adding a protocol field to the message event. Fixed, in `src/renderer/src/media/voice/speak.worker.ts:63`.

**What was happening.** kokoro's `TextSplitterStream.close()` throws if it has already been closed:

```js
close(){if(this._closed)throw new Error("Stream is already closed.");…}
```

`VoiceMouth.seal()` sends a `close` at the end of every reply, but the worker closed the splitter and kept holding it. So the next `hush()` closed the same dead stream a second time.

**Why it mattered more than a red line in the console.** `hush()` is the first thing the `open` handler runs, so the throw aborted that handler *before* `turn = message.turn`. The turn never opened, the stale splitter stayed put, and every following `open` threw in the same place. The agent went silent from the second reply onward, and nothing in the app said why. Your stack shows the `stop` path, which is the same double close when you cut in after a reply had finished.

**The change.** A closed stream is forgotten rather than kept for a later `hush` to close again:

```ts
const seal = () => {
  splitter?.close()
  splitter = null
}

const hush = () => {
  turn = NOBODY
  seal()
}
```

and the window's `close` message goes through `seal()` too. `run` holds its own reference to the stream, so it still drains the sentences already in flight and posts its `done`.

**Coverage.** The worker had none, since kokoro pulls in the whole transformers runtime. `tests/voice-speak-worker.test.ts` drives the real worker module with a stand-in splitter held to the one rule that matters, close twice and it throws, and covers a second turn opening after the first closed, a `stop` after a close, and an old turn's sentences being dropped. I reverted the fix to check the test has teeth: it fails with `Error: Stream is already closed.` at the `stop`, which is your line.

`yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean and the four voice suites pass, 45 tests. Worth a run through the real models with `yarn voice-check` before you trust it end to end, since that is the only thing that hears actual sound come out.

This preserves the existing rule that commands only open threads, though it does shift how we apply that logic.

Actually, a dedicated `spoken?: boolean` field on both `chat.send` and the message event feels more honest—it explicitly marks that the message arrived via voice without conflating it with the command system. I'd add it as a seventh parameter to `sendChat` after `commands`, keeping with the existing style, and have voice.ts pass it in both the thread-opening and regular message branches.

The tradeoff is that `sendChat(text, undefined, undefined, undefined, [agentId], ['voice'], true)` looks messy with all those undefined placeholders. Alternatively, since voice.ts is the only caller that ever sets `commands: ['voice']`, I could lean on that signal—have the in-thread voice send also pass `commands: ['voice']` and let the server treat it as a spoken marker inside threads while ignoring it for mode. That way `sendChat` stays unchanged, but I'd need to update the thread branch in store.ts to include commands in the socket send instead of dropping it. Both paths touch roughly the same number of files, so it's really about whether the explicit `spoken` field or the implicit `commands: ['voice']` signal is cleaner.

I'm leaning toward the `commands` route since it avoids widening the sendChat signature and keeps the protocol consistent—the command describes how the message was sent, and 'voice' is the one that stays meaningful inside a thread. The cleanest approach is a simple flag in the sounds module itself—something like `hushChat(on)`—that voice.ts can set when opening or closing. This avoids the circular import problem since voice already depends on sounds. I could read `useVoice.getState().open` directly in the store, but that would create a cycle too since voice.ts imports `useCrew` from store. A plain flag in the sounds module keeps things simple and follows the app's patterns.
